question: What primary role does the family unit play in the food supply chain?

options.A: It acts as the final link that consumes and utilizes the food.
options.B: It regulates international trade agreements for agricultural goods.
options.C: It determines large-scale industrial farming methods.
options.D: It sets global market prices for staple crops.

explanation: Families sit at the end of the supply chain, turning raw food into meals and nutrition for household members. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h1)

question: Why is a family often called a mini-economy when it comes to food?

options.A: Because households must carefully manage limited resources to secure daily meals.
options.B: Because families set the tax rates on imported agricultural products.
options.C: Because households export surplus food to international markets.
options.D: Because families print their own currency to buy groceries.

explanation: You got it! Just like a big economy, a family has to balance its money and resources against the everyday need to put food on the table. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h1)

question: What does a family's ability to buy food mainly depend on?

options.A: Local government policies on soil fertilization.
options.B: Total income, employment stability, and market food prices.
options.C: Global weather patterns and international shipping laws.
options.D: The distance from the nearest agricultural research center.

explanation: Exactly! Purchasing power simply means how much money is coming into the house compared to how much food actually costs in the market. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h2)

question: If a family suddenly loses income due to a job loss, what dietary change is most likely to happen first?

options.A: Stopping all food consumption completely for several days.
options.B: Switching entirely to imported gourmet food items.
options.C: Replacing expensive protein sources and fresh fruits with cheaper, starchy foods.
options.D: Growing all their own wheat and livestock in a small backyard.

explanation: Well done! When cash gets tight, families usually stretch their budget by swapping pricey proteins and fruits for filling, affordable starches. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h2)

question: What is the main benefit when a family practices subsistence farming?

options.A: It completely protects crops from all types of extreme weather.
options.B: It eliminates the need for any physical labor by family members.
options.C: It allows families to produce their own food and bypass high market prices.
options.D: It guarantees millions of dollars in profit from international exports.

explanation: Spot on! Growing your own food means you don't always need cash in hand just to feed your household. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h3)

question: Why are families who rely only on subsistence farming at risk of malnutrition?

options.A: Subsistence farmers are legally forbidden from eating their own crops.
options.B: Growing food at home causes chronic fatigue in children.
options.C: Home-grown food contains zero vitamins or minerals.
options.D: A failed harvest from drought or pests directly removes their food supply.

explanation: You got it. If bad weather or pests ruin the crops, these families lose both their meals and their fallback income all at once. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h3)

question: How does culture mostly shape what a family eats?

options.A: By defining which items are acceptable to eat and how meals are prepared.
options.B: By determining the exact daily caloric requirement of the human body.
options.C: By setting the official market price for imported grains.
options.D: By controlling the chemical composition of soil in the local region.

explanation: Exactly! Our cultural background teaches us from childhood what counts as good food and how it should be cooked. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h4)

question: A pregnant patient refuses to eat eggs due to a local tradition. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Ignore the dietary restriction since culture has no impact on health.
options.B: Scold the family for holding backward customs that harm their health.
options.C: Acknowledge her belief respectfully while discussing alternative local foods that provide the same nutrients.
options.D: Force the patient to eat eggs during her hospital admission.

explanation: Brilliant nursing judgment! Great care means respecting a patient's culture while gently finding safe, alternative ways to meet their nutritional needs. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h4)

question: What is meant by 'intra-household food distribution'?

options.A: How international organizations ship relief food to disaster zones.
options.B: How supermarkets transport goods from warehouses to neighborhood stores.
options.C: How the government distributes farming subsidies to rural communities.
options.D: How food is shared and divided among people living in the same home.

explanation: Spot on! This simply looks at who gets what share of the pot right inside your own house. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h5)

question: In many homes, unfair food sharing puts which group at the highest risk of poor nutrition?

options.A: Young children and pregnant or lactating women.
options.B: Older teenage boys who play sports.
options.D: Adult male wage earners who work outside the home.

explanation: You're right! Even though their bodies need extra nutrients for growth and health, these groups often end up with the smallest shares. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to preserve food at home?

options.A: Exposing raw meat to open air at room temperature for several days.
options.B: Drying fruits and vegetables under the sun.
options.C: Smoking or salting fish to prevent bacterial growth.
options.D: Storing perishable items in a working refrigerator.

explanation: Correct! Leaving raw meat out in the open air lets bacteria multiply fast and ruins the food instead of saving it. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h6)

question: How can poor food storage at home harm a child's health?

options.A: It lowers the market price of local vegetables.
options.B: It reduces the child's daily physical activity levels.
options.C: It automatically increases the vitamin content of stored grains.
options.D: It causes foodborne infections that trigger diarrhea and hinder nutrient absorption.

explanation: Spot on! Spoiled or contaminated food leads to tummy infections, making it hard for the child's body to keep the nutrients it needs. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h6)

question: What is a common long-term result of poor eating habits within a family?

options.A: Guaranteed immunity against all infectious diseases.
options.B: Chronic malnutrition and developmental stunting in children.
options.C: Immediate improvement in community economic status.
options.D: Increased agricultural crop yields for the next season.

explanation: You got it! Consistently missing out on key nutrients prevents growing children from reaching their full physical and mental potential. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h7)

question: Why do nurses always encourage families to eat a variety of different foods?

options.A: Diversity in meals prevents food from spoiling in storage.
options.B: Eating only one type of food is the cheapest way to survive.
options.C: Eating a wide variety of foods ensures the body gets a complete range of essential nutrients.
options.D: Eating different foods eliminates the need for clean drinking water.

explanation: Brilliant! No single food item has every nutrient our bodies need, which is why a mixed diet is the secret to good health. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T031#GNS227_U2_T031_h7)
